title: Schools close
hookLine: the tour of the world's practices ends

lines: THE LAST EVENING OF A TRIP.
cards: The last evening of a long trip has its own feeling. The bag is half packed. The host family is clearing the table.

Before the taxi, there's a moment when you can slip out with a wave, or stop in the doorway and say something real. This path's tour of the world's schools of practice ends today. Zen halls and koans.
Tibetan mind training and a sand mandala swept away. The desert, the Jesus Prayer, Quaker silence, Taizé. Kavanah, the Omer, study in pairs.
Sufi watchfulness, the eight limbs, japa, the ambrosial hour, the sangat. Qigong in a park, three daily checks, the ancestors, the porch. Now, the doorway.

teach.b: Marcus Aurelius gives a model for leaving well. The first book of his Meditations isn't philosophy at all. It's a list of thanks.
From his grandfather, he says, he learned good morals and how to govern his temper. From his mother, piety, generosity and a simple way of living. From a teacher, to bear hard work and want little.
From another, not to busy himself with trifles.

One by one, he names a person and the specific thing he received. He doesn't thank them for being wonderful in general. He thanks each for one particular gift, and in naming it, he shows he was paying attention.
And he keeps it: the list sits at the front of the notebook he wrote for himself. A tour of other people's practices deserves a thank-you like that.
Each tradition let a guest in, sometimes very far in: its prayers, its silences, its songs, its kitchens. Some kept a few doors closed, and that was theirs to decide.

teach.h: NOT A SOUVENIR FROM EVERY HOUSE.
teach.b: The respectful way to leave isn't to pack a souvenir from every house, or to pretend you now belong to all of them.
It's to stand in the doorway of one and say, specifically: from you, I learned this.
Thanks works the way yesterday's ends did. It's given to a particular tradition, for a particular gift, without measuring it against any other. That's what makes it more than politeness.

how: Guests at another tradition's practices may thank their hosts before leaving; the first book of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations is a list of thanks, naming each person and the particular thing he learned from them.

the tour's end, left with thanks for one named gift

games.q: it's the last evening of your stay with a host family. the taxi is waiting. what do you do?
o: take a keepsake from every room.
slip out with a quick wave.
stop in the doorway and thank them for one particular thing.
games.why: Marcus Aurelius opens his notebook this way: one person, one gift, named precisely. a thank-you that proves you were listening.

practice: Let the tour pass through your mind, house by house, and stop at the one that gave you something you still use or still think about.

Name the tradition, then name the gift as precisely as Marcus did: not "it was beautiful," but the actual thing, a way of breathing, a line, a habit, a question. Silently, thank the people who kept it and passed it down.

wordCard.voice: Schools close. The end of this path's tour of the world's schools of practice, left the way Marcus Aurelius began his notebook: with specific thanks. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: thank you. One gift, named precisely, says more than a souvenir from every house. Thanks for walking it with me.
